1

Reading · learning a language

1.1 Discuss. How long have you been learning English? What is the fastest progress you have ever made, and why?

KEY WORDS

fluent able to speak easily and well

immersion surrounding yourself with a language

a plateau a period with no visible progress

intensive done with great effort in a short time

Can You Really Learn a Language in 22 Hours?

A few years ago, a British journalist set himself an unusual challenge. Using memory techniques borrowed from competitive memorisers, he tried to learn enough Spanish in twenty-two hours to hold a conversation. At the end, he sat down with a native speaker and — slowly, imperfectly, but genuinely — talked for half an hour. The experiment made headlines. It also annoyed a great many language teachers.

The teachers had a point. What the journalist had actually built was a small, well-organised set of words and phrases, arranged so that his brain could find them quickly. That is a real skill, and a useful one. But it is not the same as understanding a fast argument between two strangers on a bus, or reading a newspaper column, or catching the joke in a film. Those things depend on thousands of hours of exposure, not on clever storage.

Still, the experiment revealed something that ordinary learners often miss: most people are not slow at languages, they are simply inefficient. They spend months revising material they already know, avoid speaking because it is uncomfortable, and treat vocabulary as a list to be memorised rather than a system to be used. Change those three habits and progress accelerates sharply — not to twenty-two hours, but far faster than most people expect.

Researchers who study successful learners find the same patterns again and again. They test themselves instead of rereading. They speak early and badly rather than waiting until they feel ready. They learn words in phrases, not alone. And crucially, they accept the plateau: the long, flat middle period when improvement is invisible but real, and when most learners quietly give up.

So can you learn a language in twenty-two hours? No. But the honest question is more useful: are you learning as well as you could be? For most people, the answer is no — and that is far better news than it sounds.

2

Grammar · present simple and present continuous

PRESENTATION

PRESENT SIMPLE — permanent situations, habits, facts:

She teaches English. · I get up at seven. · Water boils at 100°C.

PRESENT CONTINUOUS — now, temporary situations, changing situations:

She is teaching a class right now. · I am living with my aunt this month. · The climate is changing.

Present simple

Present continuous

always, usually, often, every day

now, at the moment, this week, currently

I speak three languages.

I'm speaking Spanish today for practice.

He works in a bank.

He's working from home this month.

The bus leaves at six.

The situation is getting better.

ERROR WARNING

State verbs are not normally used in the continuous:

know, understand, believe, want, need, like, love, hate, own, seem, mean

I am knowing the answer. ✗ I know the answer. ✓

She is wanting to leave. ✗ She wants to leave. ✓

But think and have change meaning: I think it's true (opinion) · I'm thinking about it (activity).

4

Everyday English · giving and responding to opinions

4.1 Read the conversation.

Sardor So what did you think of the new language app?

Malika To be honest, I wasn't impressed. It just repeats word lists.

Sardor Really? I thought it was quite useful.

Malika Well, the pronunciation practice is good, I'll give you that.

Sardor Exactly! And it's free, don't you think that matters?

Malika Hmm, I'm not so sure. Free things waste your time too.

Sardor That's a fair point. Maybe it works better for beginners.

Malika Yes — I'd agree with that.

Giving an opinion

Agreeing

Disagreeing politely

To be honest, …

Exactly!

Really? I thought…

I thought (it was)…

Me too. / Me neither.

I'm not so sure.

If you ask me, …

That's a fair point.

I see what you mean, but…

ERROR WARNING

Me too after a positive statement · me neither after a negative one:

“I loved it.” — “Me too.” “I didn't like it.” — “Me neither.”
